paragraphs: Clustering a continuous stream of high-dimensional data becomes difficult when only a small number of observations can remain in memory. This paper studies what can still be learned when comparisons between observations are available only within a limited window. Those comparisons form a banded kernel matrix, with entries outside the accessible window set to zero.

The authors develop a random matrix framework for understanding this matrix in a large-dimensional regime. They derive the limiting distribution of its eigenvalues and investigate isolated eigenvalues and their associated eigenvectors. These spectral features behave differently from familiar settings, making their analysis important for understanding how restricted memory changes the information available for clustering.

The paper uses these results to construct efficient online kernel spectral clustering methods and provide theoretical performance guarantees. Image clustering experiments support the analysis. The contribution connects a concrete resource constraint to the mathematical behavior of the clustering machinery, offering guidance for processing high-dimensional streams when retaining and comparing the full dataset is impractical.
icml-2022-a-random-matrix-analysis-of-da.tldr: A random matrix analysis explains how limited memory changes streaming spectral clustering and supports efficient methods with theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: High-dimensional bandit problems involve repeatedly choosing actions while learning which choices yield good rewards. Although the unknown parameters may have many coordinates, useful structure can make the underlying problem much smaller. This paper develops a unified algorithm for stochastic bandit problems with such low-dimensional structure, motivated by applications including online advertising and drug discovery.

The central idea is to use that structure to guide parameter estimation. Rather than analyzing each structured problem entirely separately, the authors provide a general framework for bounding regret, the cost of making decisions while learning. Under a shared set of assumptions described as mild, the same algorithm and analysis apply across several high-dimensional settings.

For the LASSO bandit, the framework recovers comparable regret bounds as a check on its behavior. It also produces new bounds with logarithmic dependence on dimension for low-rank matrix bandits, group sparse matrix bandits, and a newly introduced multi-agent LASSO bandit. These results show how one analytical approach can capture benefits from several different forms of low-dimensional structure.
icml-2022-a-simple-unified-framework-for.tldr: A unified bandit algorithm exploits low-dimensional structure to obtain regret guarantees across several high-dimensional settings.

paragraphs: A point cloud represents an object or observation through a collection of points. Comparing such collections often requires more than a distance: applications may also need meaningful angles, volumes, or derivatives. This paper develops a geometric framework that defines these quantities without making their meaning depend on the chosen coordinates.

The authors interpret the points within each cloud as samples from an underlying probability density. Each entire cloud then becomes a point on a statistical manifold, a space whose elements represent probability-based objects. The Fisher information metric supplies the geometry of this space, providing a common mathematical basis for measuring and manipulating point clouds.

The framework is applied to two autoencoder tasks. One smoothly transforms a three-dimensional object into another by interpolating between their point clouds. The other learns latent coordinates that preserve angles and distances, aiming for a more discriminative representation. Experiments on large standard point-cloud benchmarks report substantial classification improvements over existing methods. The results connect richer geometric descriptions to useful learned representations.
icml-2022-a-statistical-manifold-framewo.tldr: Treating point clouds as probability-based geometric objects enables smooth interpolation and latent representations with improved classification results.

paragraphs: This paper develops sampling algorithms for distributions whose convex potential combines a continuously differentiable term with a term that may be nonsmooth. The nonsmooth component complicates methods that rely on ordinary gradients. The authors address this setting through Langevin Monte Carlo algorithms built from tools in convex analysis and optimization.

Their approach uses Bregman–Moreau envelopes to smoothly approximate the nonsmooth component and Bregman proximity operators to handle its structure. These tools are paired with Langevin methods resembling mirror descent. The resulting framework extends existing methods both by allowing mirror-descent-like sampling of nonsmooth distributions and by replacing the usual Moreau smoothing with its more general Bregman counterpart.

A particular instance of the proposed scheme resembles a Bregman proximal gradient algorithm, connecting the sampling procedure to an optimization method. The authors illustrate efficiency on several sampling tasks where existing Langevin Monte Carlo methods are known to struggle. The contribution is a broader algorithmic toolkit for this class of convex sampling problems, supported by demonstrations on challenging tasks.
icml-2022-bregman-proximal-langevin-mont.tldr: Bregman smoothing and proximity operators extend Langevin sampling to nonsmooth convex distributions using mirror-descent-like algorithms.

paragraphs: Source-free unsupervised domain adaptation transfers a pretrained model to an unlabeled target domain without accessing its original training data. A central difficulty is that labels inferred by the model can be wrong. Giving every target example equal importance allows these incorrect pseudo-labels to influence adaptation as strongly as more reliable ones.

The paper introduces the Joint Model-Data Structure score, or JMDS, to assign confidence separately to each example. It combines knowledge from the source model with knowledge from the target domain, whereas the compared confidence approaches use only one of these sources. This makes the score a way to distinguish how much individual target samples should contribute to learning.

The authors incorporate these scores as sample weights in CoWA-JMDS and add weight Mixup, a variant designed to encourage greater use of target-domain knowledge. Experiments report better confidence scoring than existing alternatives and state-of-the-art adaptation performance across closed, open, and partial-set scenarios. The findings support combining model knowledge and target structure when deciding which unlabeled examples to trust.
icml-2022-confidence-score-for-source-fr.tldr: JMDS combines source-model and target-domain knowledge to weight unlabeled examples and improve source-free domain adaptation.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether policy-gradient learning reaches a globally optimal solution in entropy-regularized decision problems. The setting has an infinite time horizon and continuous state and action spaces. Policies use a softmax representation with a one-hidden-layer neural network, analyzed in a mean-field regime through a probability measure describing the network.

The authors add entropy regularization to that mean-field measure and examine the resulting gradient flow using the 2-Wasserstein metric. They prove that the objective increases along this flow. When the additional regularization is sufficiently strong, the flow converges exponentially fast to a unique stationary solution, which is also the unique maximizer of the regularized objective.

The paper also examines how the value function along training responds to regularization parameters and initialization. Its analysis relies on a nonlinear Fokker–Planck–Kolmogorov equation and extends convergence research from tabular policies to the stated neural approximation setting. The sufficient-regularization condition is central: the global convergence result concerns this particular regularized mean-field flow.
icml-2022-convergence-of-policy-gradient.tldr: With sufficient additional mean-field regularization, a neural policy-gradient flow converges exponentially to the unique optimum of its regularized objective.

paragraphs: Dataset condensation creates a small synthetic training set intended to retain useful information from a larger dataset. This paper identifies a failure of approaches based on matching gradients separately for each class. The authors prove that existing methods can underperform random selection when a substantial part of the training data consists of task-irrelevant information.

They attribute the problem to missing signals about differences between classes. Their method, Dataset Condensation with Contrastive signals, changes the loss so that these differences participate in the condensation process. The paper also studies the new loss through training dynamics by tracking kernel velocity, and introduces a bi-level warm-up procedure to stabilize optimization.

Experiments show that the proposed method creates informative synthetic datasets for fine-grained image classification tasks where the existing methods evaluated are ineffective. It also outperforms the tested baselines on SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, and is applied to continual learning. Together, the findings support making class distinctions explicit when deciding which information a condensed dataset should preserve.
icml-2022-dataset-condensation-with-cont.tldr: Adding between-class contrastive signals helps dataset condensation retain useful information when class-wise gradient matching can fail.

paragraphs: The Maximal Information Coefficient, or MIC, measures dependence between variables. Publishing it for sensitive data can reveal private information, creating a need for a privacy-preserving alternative. This paper investigates how to approximate MIC under differential privacy while keeping the resulting statistic accurate enough to be useful.

The authors show that directly applying the classic Laplace mechanism produces insufficient accuracy. They introduce a different approximation, MICr, designed to work better with differential privacy, and construct two private versions. They also prove that MICr consistently estimates MIC, giving the underlying approximation a statistical foundation as the amount of data grows.

Experiments on real and synthetic datasets show that the private MICr statistics substantially outperform the direct Laplace approach. On real datasets, the reported accuracy becomes usable when sample sizes are at least moderately large. The work illustrates why designing a statistic around privacy requirements can matter: the choice of quantity being privatized affects how much useful dependence information survives the privacy mechanism.
icml-2022-differentially-private-maximal.tldr: A new MIC approximation enables differentially private dependence estimates with better empirical accuracy than directly applying Laplace noise.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to compare Gaussian distributions that may occupy spaces of different dimensions. It considers entropy-regularized Gromov–Wasserstein transport and an unbalanced variant. The analysis focuses on the inner-product formulation, called IGW, so its conclusions concern that particular way of comparing the internal structure of distributions.

The authors show that optimal transport plans for entropic IGW between Gaussian distributions are themselves Gaussian, with an analogous result for the unbalanced version. This identifies the form of the optimal solution. Using von Neumann’s trace inequality, they then obtain closed-form expressions for the entropic IGW comparison between the distributions.

The paper also studies a barycenter, a representative distribution for several Gaussian inputs under this transport criterion. It proves that this barycenter is Gaussian when the entropy-regularization parameter is small, and derives an explicit formula for its covariance matrix. Together, the results turn these transport and averaging questions into analytically characterized problems within the stated Gaussian and inner-product setting.
icml-2022-entropic-gromov-wasserstein-be.tldr: For Gaussian inputs, entropic inner-product Gromov–Wasserstein transport has Gaussian optimal plans and closed-form expressions.

paragraphs: Strategic classification studies prediction when people can change their features to obtain outcomes they prefer. Many existing models assume everyone wants a positive prediction, as might occur with loan approval. This paper argues that this assumption captures only a limited range of user interests and develops a more flexible account of strategic behavior.

The proposed generalized model includes most current models while allowing additional settings. The authors focus especially on cases where users and the predictive system have aligned interests. Even there, they find that standard maximum-margin losses are poorly suited to strategic inputs. Shared goals therefore do not by themselves make a conventional training objective appropriate.

Returning to the broader model, the paper introduces a maximum-margin framework designed for strategic learning and provides theoretical analysis. Experiments demonstrate its practical utility. The contribution combines a broader description of what users want with a learning approach that accounts for their ability to respond to predictions, making the interaction between incentives and training objectives explicit.
icml-2022-generalized-strategic-classifi.tldr: A broader model of user incentives motivates a strategic maximum-margin framework, including cases where users and the system share goals.

paragraphs: Group-equivariant convolutional networks encode symmetries such as rotations and permutations in their architecture. This paper examines an additional influence on what they learn: the implicit preference introduced by gradient descent. Its central question is how training selects among possible solutions even beyond the symmetry constraints explicitly built into the network.

For full-width linear networks with L layers trained for binary classification, the authors show convergence to solutions with low-rank Fourier matrix coefficients, characterized by a 2/L-Schatten matrix norm. The result extends earlier analysis of linear convolutional networks to all finite groups, including noncommutative groups such as permutations, and to band-limited networks over infinite groups.

Experiments across several groups validate the theoretical results. The authors also explore nonlinear networks empirically and observe similar regularization patterns locally, a more qualified finding than the linear-network theorem. Finally, uncertainty principles help interpret the Fourier-space behavior in the original representation space. The work links network depth, encoded symmetry, and training-induced structure within one mathematical account.
icml-2022-implicit-bias-of-linear-equiva.tldr: Gradient descent on specified linear equivariant networks favors low-rank Fourier structure, with a regularization pattern determined by depth.

paragraphs: Regression is sometimes performed on a smaller sketch of a dataset instead of the full sample. This paper asks how that choice affects statistical inference when regression errors have unequal variances. In the full dataset, such heteroskedasticity would ordinarily call for robust standard errors to support accurate tests.

The authors show that estimates from random-projection sketches can behave as though the errors had constant variance. Random sampling does not share this property. Their explanation expresses the projected-data estimates as degenerate U-statistics and establishes that, under certain conditions, these statistics have asymptotically normal distributions with a homoskedastic form of variance.

The paper verifies the relevant conditions for least squares with exogenous covariates and for instrumental variables estimation with endogenous covariates. The implication is that an appropriately chosen sketch can simplify inference as well as reduce the data used for estimation. This is an asymptotic result under the stated conditions; its significance lies in how the sketching mechanism changes the estimator’s statistical behavior.
icml-2022-least-squares-estimation-using.tldr: Under stated conditions, random-projection sketches yield regression estimates with homoskedastic-form asymptotic variance even when original errors are heteroskedastic.

paragraphs: This paper improves deep convolutional network inference under fully homomorphic encryption using the RNS-CKKS scheme. A previous implementation had demonstrated ResNet-20 with bootstrapping, but high latency and a low security level limited its practicality. The authors target computational cost and numerical stability while achieving standard 128-bit security.

Their multiplexed parallel convolution packs sparse outputs from multiple channels compactly to reduce total bootstrapping time. They also introduce imaginary-removing bootstrapping to prevent catastrophic divergence during approximate ReLU operations. Additional changes optimize level consumption and use lighter, tighter parameters, addressing several interacting costs of running deep networks in the encrypted setting.

Simulation results report 4.67-fold lower inference latency and 134-fold lower runtime per image for ResNet-20 relative to the previous state of the art. These measure different aspects of efficiency: latency and amortized processing cost. The authors also report the first successful high-accuracy ResNet-110 implementation on RNS-CKKS. The findings demonstrate progress in both the efficiency and supported depth of encrypted neural inference.
icml-2022-low-complexity-deep-convolutio.tldr: Compact parallel convolutions and improved bootstrapping reduce encrypted ResNet inference costs while achieving 128-bit security.

paragraphs: Rare events sit in the tails of a probability distribution, where training examples are scarce. Generative models can consequently focus on the more densely sampled central region and represent extremes poorly. This paper aims to improve how normalizing flows learn tail behavior, making their probability models more accurate in these sparsely observed regions.

The key theoretical result concerns autoregressive flows: the tail behavior of individual output variables can be controlled through the corresponding tail properties of the base distribution. This gives the authors a direct design principle for the model. They build a new type of flow using flexible base distributions together with data-driven linear layers.

The empirical analysis reports improved accuracy, especially in the tails, and shows that the method can generate heavy-tailed data. A weather and climate application illustrates a setting where representing extremes is essential. The contribution combines a mathematical explanation of how tail behavior can be controlled with a model design that uses that control in practice.
icml-2022-marginal-tail-adaptive-normali.tldr: Flexible base distributions give autoregressive normalizing flows control over marginal tails and improve empirical modeling of extreme observations.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a neural network to acquire new tasks while retaining earlier ones. A puzzling observation is that forgetting does not simply grow as tasks become more different. Instead, it appears most severe when tasks have an intermediate degree of similarity. This paper seeks a theoretical explanation for that pattern.

The authors analyze both a synthetic teacher-student framework and a real-data setup. Their explanation, called the Maslow’s Hammer hypothesis, centers on a trade-off between activating nodes and reusing nodes. The analysis connects this trade-off to the intermediate-similarity regime where forgetting is worst, giving task similarity a more nuanced role in interference.

The paper then uses this account to reinterpret popular interventions against catastrophic forgetting. It identifies the regimes in which those interventions are most effective through their relationship to activation and reuse. The contribution is an explanation that helps organize existing methods: understanding how tasks engage network nodes provides a basis for assessing when a particular intervention is likely to help.
icml-2022-maslows-hammer-in-catastrophic.tldr: A trade-off between node activation and reuse explains why forgetting can peak at intermediate task similarity.

paragraphs: Batch policy optimization learns a decision rule from a fixed dataset containing only partial feedback. This paper asks how to choose among several model classes so that the resulting policy competes with the policy from the best class. It formalizes this selection problem for contextual bandits with linear model classes.

The authors identify three considerations: approximation error, statistical complexity, and coverage. The first two concern how well a class can represent a good solution and how difficult it is to estimate from data. Coverage adds a distinct challenge because the available dataset may not adequately support the decisions a learned policy would make.

The paper proves that no algorithm in this setting can obtain the desired guarantee for all three considerations simultaneously. However, relaxing any one allows algorithms with near-oracle guarantees for the remaining two. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these approaches. The results explain why model selection here needs explicit compromises beyond the familiar balance between model fit and complexity in supervised learning.
icml-2022-model-selection-in-batch-polic.tldr: Batch policy model selection cannot optimally address approximation, complexity, and coverage together, but relaxing one enables strong guarantees for the other two.

paragraphs: Much theoretical progress on neural network training has focused on networks with very large width. That emphasis leaves depth less directly addressed. This paper instead studies narrow networks as their depth grows without bound, asking whether training can be guaranteed in a regime where depth is the central source of overparameterization.

The authors begin with a multilayer perceptron under a specific initialization. They analyze its infinite-depth limit using neural tangent kernel theory and establish a trainability guarantee. The initialization is part of the stated setting, so the result provides a guarantee for this construction rather than an unrestricted claim about every deep, narrow network.

The analysis is then extended to an infinitely deep convolutional network, accompanied by brief experiments. The authors present the work as the first trainability guarantee for infinitely deep but narrow networks. Its main contribution is to expand the theoretical study of training beyond the wide-network regime, showing that a depth-focused limit can also support a mathematical guarantee.
icml-2022-neural-tangent-kernel-analysis.tldr: Neural tangent kernel analysis establishes trainability for infinitely deep, narrow networks under a specific initialization.

paragraphs: This paper views a neural network’s learned connection weights as a program specifying how it processes data. In an ordinary network, training on new data changes that program and can overwrite previous learning. Neurocoder introduces an architecture that stores modular neural programs in external memory and composes them according to the current data.

The central idea is to treat programs themselves as stored data. Relevant modules can be shared and combined, allowing the network to configure its computation responsively. This makes program reuse an explicit architectural capability, including the possibility of building more complex programs from simpler ones rather than learning every computation as a single undivided set of weights.

Integrated into existing neural architectures, Neurocoder demonstrates modular learning, composition, handling of pattern shifts, and retention of old programs while learning new ones. The authors report substantial performance improvements in object recognition, video games, and continual learning tasks. These findings support stored, reusable programs as a practical mechanism for broadening what a neural architecture can retain and recombine.
icml-2022-neurocoder-general-purpose-com.tldr: Neurocoder stores and combines reusable neural programs to adapt computation and improve performance across recognition, games, and continual learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies adversarial attacks on discrete sequences when an attacker can query a model but cannot inspect its internals. With limited queries, deciding which sequence positions to change is important. Existing greedy approaches often preselect important positions, restricting the search and potentially missing better adversarial examples.

The proposed method uses Bayesian optimization with an automatic relevance determination categorical kernel to update which positions matter during the search. To make this approach scale to longer sequences, the authors add block decomposition and subsampling of search history. A separate post-optimization procedure seeks adversarial examples requiring fewer changes.

Experiments on natural-language and protein classification tasks report consistently higher attack success rates than the previous state-of-the-art methods evaluated, alongside substantial reductions in query count and modification rate. The results connect three goals: finding successful attacks, limiting model queries, and keeping changes small. The main methodological contribution is a search process that adapts its view of important positions while addressing the computational demands of long sequences.
icml-2022-query-efficient-and-scalable-b.tldr: Adaptive Bayesian optimization finds discrete-sequence adversarial examples with higher empirical success and fewer queries and modifications.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as Adam can make deep-network training robust, but require extra memory. This paper asks whether ordinary stochastic gradient descent can obtain similar benefits through architectural changes. Its proposed recipe makes the architecture scale invariant and trains it with SGD and weight decay.

The recipe optionally clips the global gradient norm using a threshold proportional to the weight norm times the square root of twice the weight decay divided by the learning rate. The authors prove robustness to parameter and loss rescaling: convergence depends only logarithmically on initialization and loss scales. By comparison, standard SGD may fail to converge for many initializations.

To demonstrate the approach, the authors construct SIBERT, a scale-invariant version of BERT. Trained with vanilla SGD, it achieves downstream-task performance comparable to BERT trained with adaptive methods such as Adam. The contribution links an architectural property to optimization robustness, showing how changing the network can help a memory-efficient optimizer work effectively in the reported setting.
icml-2022-robust-training-of-neural-netw.tldr: Scale-invariant architectures let SGD with weight decay train robustly, with SIBERT matching adaptive-optimizer BERT performance on reported downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Mean field games approximate strategic interactions within very large populations. Learning their equilibria with reinforcement learning presents a practical obstacle: existing algorithms need to mix estimated strategies or action values. That operation becomes difficult when the estimates are represented by nonlinear models such as neural networks.

The paper proposes two ways to handle this mixing. The first distills historical data into a neural network that represents a mixed strategy, and applies this procedure to Fictitious Play. The second uses regularization to mix information online without storing historical data or previous estimates, and extends Online Mirror Descent.

These approaches address the interface between equilibrium-learning algorithms and neural function approximation. Numerical experiments show that they efficiently enable deep reinforcement learning to solve several mean field games and outperform state-of-the-art baselines from the literature. Their significance is in making the required mixing operation workable with neural networks, while offering both a history-based method and an online alternative that avoids retaining earlier data or estimates.
icml-2022-scalable-deep-reinforcement-le.tldr: Distillation and online regularization make strategy mixing compatible with deep reinforcement learning for mean field games.

paragraphs: Vision models built from multilayer perceptrons need to mix information across image locations and feature channels. The paper identifies inefficient mixing between these dimensions as a reason such models can require extensive pretraining. It approaches the problem through knowledge distillation, aiming to improve how these architectures exchange information.

The proposed Spatial-channel Token Distillation method introduces distillation tokens for both spatial and channel dimensions. A mutual information regularizer encourages the tokens to focus on their respective dimensions. Together, these components organize the distillation process around the two kinds of information mixing that the authors seek to improve.

ImageNet experiments across several MLP-like architectures show accuracy improvements. Mixer-S16 rises from 73.8% to 75.7% top-1 accuracy without costly JFT-300M pretraining. The authors also report gains of about 1.1 and 0.5 percentage points for CycleMLP-B1 and CycleMLP-B2. These results indicate that the mechanism can benefit both the highlighted Mixer model and stronger architectures, with the reported improvement varying by architecture.
icml-2022-spatial-channel-token-distilla.tldr: Spatial and channel distillation tokens improve vision MLP accuracy, including Mixer-S16 gains without JFT-300M pretraining.

paragraphs: Implicit stochastic gradient descent is a proximal version of SGD that has attracted interest for its stability. This paper examines how to use it for statistical inference about model parameters, where estimating a parameter is only part of the task. Reliable uncertainty estimates are also needed to construct confidence intervals.

For smooth convex functions, the authors analyze two procedures: proximal Robbins–Monro and proximal Polyak–Ruppert. They derive finite-sample bounds on point-estimation error and characterize the limiting distributions of the estimates. They also introduce online estimators of the corresponding asymptotic covariance matrices, each requiring only a single run of implicit SGD.

Those covariance estimates support valid confidence intervals for model parameters. The analysis removes the generalized-linear-model assumption that constrained preceding work, while retaining the stated smooth convex setting. The authors describe their online covariance estimators as apparently the first of their kind for implicit SGD. The contribution connects stable iterative estimation with practical uncertainty quantification during the same optimization run.
icml-2022-statistical-inference-with-imp.tldr: Analysis of two implicit SGD procedures yields error bounds, limiting distributions, and single-run online covariance estimates for confidence intervals.

paragraphs: Standard generalization theory often asks whether average training loss accurately reflects average loss on new data. Risk-sensitive learning may instead care about other properties of the loss distribution. This paper develops guarantees for a broad class of Hölder risk functionals, whose values remain close when the corresponding cumulative loss distributions are close.

The authors establish uniform convergence for estimates of the loss distribution’s cumulative distribution function. This leads to guarantees that hold simultaneously across a hypothesis class and a class of risk functionals. The shared distributional argument provides a way to justify empirical risk minimization for multiple risk criteria within one framework.

The paper also develops gradient-based methods for minimizing distortion risks and proves convergence guarantees. This family includes the mean, conditional value at risk, and cumulative prospect theory risks. Experiments demonstrate the learning procedure in settings covered by uniform convergence results and in high-dimensional deep networks. The latter provide empirical evidence, while the theoretical guarantees apply in their stated settings.
icml-2022-supervised-learning-with-gener.tldr: Uniform control of loss distributions supports generalization guarantees and optimization methods for a broad family of risk-sensitive learning objectives.

paragraphs: Random partition models underpin Bayesian clustering methods used in mixture models, topic models, and community detection. Their behavior concerns both how many clusters they create and how evenly observations are distributed among those clusters. This paper develops a theoretical framework for the second property, which has received comparatively little attention.

The framework examines how exchangeable partition models assign probabilities to partitions with different degrees of balance. The authors show that the rich-get-richer behavior of many popular models follows inevitably from two assumptions taken together: product-form exchangeability and projectivity. This identifies a structural source of the preference for already-large clusters.

The paper also proposes a principled way to compare models by balancedness and introduces rich-get-poorer partition models. An application to entity resolution illustrates their use. The contribution makes cluster-size preferences an explicit modeling consideration, providing tools to understand how common assumptions shape partitions and to compare alternatives for applications where a different balance between cluster sizes is appropriate.
icml-2022-why-the-rich-get-richer-on-the.tldr: A balancedness framework shows how two common partition-model assumptions force rich-get-richer behavior and motivates rich-get-poorer alternatives.
